title: Fabric Spark Toolkit — nb_metadata_sqldb_prototype: a working metadata framework prototype on Fabric SQL Database (first-party executable notebook, 14 cells, real DDL and every statement genuinely executed against a local SQLite equivalent proving the schema)
summary: A 14-cell, first-party executable notebook implementing a complete metadata-driven ingestion framework schema — etl_source, etl_entity, etl_watermark, etl_run_log, dq_rules, and a vw_active_entities view — as real, executed DDL and DML against a local SQLite stand-in that mirrors the intended Fabric SQL Database T-SQL exactly, so every statement in the notebook genuinely runs and is checked with assertions rather than only described. The knowledge base already holds this toolkit's abstract touch-metadata-twice orchestration principle and forward-only watermark guard from prior sources, so this extraction is narrow: the concrete five-table schema itself (with its specific column purposes), the pyodbc-plus-Entra-token connection mechanics for the real Fabric SQL Database path, and the notebook's own executed proof that a disabled entity is correctly excluded from the cached active-entity set and that an attempted backwards watermark write is silently rejected by the upsert guard.
audience: Fabric platform engineers standing up a metadata-driven ingestion framework on Fabric SQL Database who need the concrete table shapes, the connection boilerplate for pyodbc against a Fabric SQL Database using an Entra access token, and executed proof that the forward-only watermark guard actually holds under a direct attack (an explicit backwards write attempt), not just a description of the pattern.
why_it_matters: The toolkit's orchestration philosophy (fetch metadata once, cache it, write run-log and watermark updates in batches) has been documented in the abstract elsewhere in the knowledge base, but this notebook is the concrete schema and connection code that makes that philosophy buildable: five specific tables with specific columns (including a JSON table_properties column for Delta-specific settings and an engine_hint column that lets an orchestrator route entities to Python versus Spark), a view that pre-joins and pre-filters to only enabled entities so worker notebooks embed no filter logic of their own, and the two real Fabric SQL Database connection gotchas — token byte-packing format and ODBC driver-name probing — that produce an opaque login failure if handled incorrectly. Its own executed run also directly attacks its own forward-only watermark guard with a backwards write and confirms the guard holds, which is a stronger form of evidence than a stated design rule.
takeaways: The prototype's five-table metadata schema separates source-level connection metadata (etl_source: source_kind, a Key-Vault-secret-name column never holding a value, base_location, default_format) from entity-level load configuration (etl_entity: target_table, layer, load_type, merge_keys, watermark_column, cluster_by, a JSON table_properties column for Delta-specific settings like deletion vectors and CDF, and an engine_hint column of spark or python that lets an orchestrator route work by engine) — plus separate etl_watermark, etl_run_log, and dq_rules tables and a vw_active_entities view that pre-joins source and entity and pre-filters to only enabled rows.

A real Fabric SQL Database connection from a notebook via pyodbc requires packing the Entra access token as UTF-16-LE bytes with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix into the connection's attrs_before dict at key 1256 (SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN) — a specific byte-packing format that produces an opaque login failure rather than a clear error message if done incorrectly.

The Fabric runtime image's installed ODBC driver name for SQL Server varies across runtime versions, so a pyodbc connection should probe pyodbc.drivers() for an available 'ODBC Driver ... for SQL Server' entry and select the most recent match rather than hard-coding a specific driver-name string.

The prototype's real executed run proved the enabled-filter and forward-only watermark guard both hold under direct test: caching the view's output correctly excluded a disabled entity from the active working set (a seeded, deliberately-disabled third entity never appeared in the cached config), and an explicit attempt to write an earlier date as a new watermark value for an entity was silently rejected by the upsert's WHERE-guarded ON CONFLICT clause, leaving the existing, later watermark value unchanged.

The prototype writes its run-log rows in one batched executemany() call at the end of a run rather than one round trip per entity, and performs its watermark upsert as a single guarded statement per entity (a MERGE in the T-SQL form, an ON CONFLICT ... WHERE guard in the SQLite equivalent) rather than an unconditional UPDATE — the same touch-the-store-twice-per-run shape as this toolkit's other metadata-driven notebooks, here proven against genuinely executing SQL rather than only described.

The prototype's gotchas checklist calls out that Fabric SQL Database connections opened inside one notebookutils.runMultiple() activity are not shareable with a concurrent activity in the same DAG — each activity should open its own connection and close it in a finally block — and that Fabric SQL Database's mirroring to OneLake is near-real-time rather than synchronous, so control-plane metadata reads should go direct via pyodbc while only downstream analytical reads should rely on the OneLake mirror.

claims.text: This notebook's real, executed metadata framework prototype schema for Fabric SQL Database separates source-level connection metadata (an etl_source table holding source_kind, a Key-Vault-secret-name column that is never the secret value itself, base_location, and default_format) from entity-level load configuration (an etl_entity table holding target_table, layer, load_type, a comma-separated merge_keys list, watermark_column, cluster_by, a JSON table_properties column for Delta-specific settings such as deletion vectors and Change Data Feed, and an engine_hint column of 'spark' or 'python' that lets an orchestrator route each entity to the right engine) — plus a separate etl_watermark table (one row per entity, so the hot read at run start is a single-row lookup), an etl_run_log table, a dq_rules table for per-entity data-quality checks, and a vw_active_entities view that pre-joins source and entity and pre-filters to rows where both are enabled, so worker notebooks embed no filter logic of their own.

A real Fabric SQL Database connection from a notebook via pyodbc requires packing the Entra access token (obtained via notebookutils.credentials.getToken against the https://database.windows.net/ resource) as UTF-16-LE-encoded bytes with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix, then passing that packed value in the connection's attrs_before dict at integer key 1256 (the SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN constant) — an incorrect byte-packing format at this step produces an opaque login failure rather than a clear, actionable error message.

The SQL Server ODBC driver name installed in a Fabric runtime image is not constant across runtime versions, so a pyodbc connection to Fabric SQL Database should probe pyodbc.drivers() at connect time for available 'ODBC Driver ... for SQL Server' entries and select the most recent match, rather than hard-coding a specific driver-name string that may not exist in every runtime image.

This notebook's real executed run directly attacked its own forward-only watermark guard by attempting to write an earlier date as a new watermark value for an entity whose watermark was already later, and confirmed the value was left unchanged: the upsert statement's WHERE-guarded ON CONFLICT clause (WHERE existing value IS NULL OR the new value is greater) silently rejected the backwards write rather than merely being described as forward-only, which the notebook frames as necessary because two interleaved runs of the same entity under a naive last-writer-wins update could otherwise silently rewind the high-water mark.

This notebook's real executed run also proved its enabled-entity filtering correct: after seeding three entities with one deliberately marked disabled, caching the vw_active_entities view's output in memory produced exactly two active entities and the disabled third entity never appeared in the cached working set, confirming the view's pre-filter (rather than per-worker filter logic) is what excludes disabled entities from processing.

This notebook's gotchas checklist states that a Fabric SQL Database connection opened inside one notebookutils.runMultiple() activity is not safely shareable with a concurrent activity running in the same DAG, so each activity should open its own connection and close it in a finally block rather than reusing a connection object across concurrently executing activities.

This notebook's gotchas checklist states that Fabric SQL Database's mirroring of its data to OneLake is near-real-time rather than synchronous with each write, so a metadata framework's own control-plane reads and writes (config lookups, run-log inserts, watermark upserts) should go direct against the SQL Database via pyodbc rather than through the OneLake mirror, while only downstream analytical consumers reading the mirrored data for reporting purposes should rely on the mirror.
